addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- anti-pattern-czar: Identify and fix error handling anti-patterns systematically. Run the detector, analyze results, fix CRITICAL issues first, then HIGH/MEDIUM. Use when asked to "fix error handling", "find anti-patterns", "error handling audit", "silent catch", "swallowed errors", or "anti-pattern cleanup". Proactively suggest when the user mentions silent failures, empty catches, or debugging nightmares caused by swallowed errors.
- chroma: Open-source embedding database for AI applications. Store embeddings and metadata, perform vector and full-text search, filter by metadata. Simple 4-function API. Scales from notebooks to production clusters. Use for semantic search, RAG applications, or document retrieval. Best for local development and open-source projects.
- competitor-analysis: Run a competitor analysis against claude-mem. Clones a competitor repo, researches it deeply, pulls claude-mem context from mem-search, writes a detailed comparison report, and publishes to cmem-discussions.
- product-analysis: Deep-dive analysis of any product, project, or tool. Clones the repo, researches it thoroughly, pulls claude-mem context from mem-search, writes a detailed analysis of what it is and how it relates to claude-mem, and publishes to cmem-discussions.
- standup: Convene the recently-active git worktrees as named agents in a markdown group
chat, have them reconcile what each changed, and converge on ONE consolidated
worktree. Each branch is an agent that posts to a shared STANDUP.md (YAML front
matter holds the GOAL + PROMPT; the body is the chat log), then the room agrees
on a merge order and a single consolidation plan in the SUMMATION. The room is
filled either by time window (past 1h / 4h / 24h / 7d / all — only worktrees
active in it join, so a 40-worktree machine collapses to the handful you
actually touched) or by hand-picking specific worktrees and/or open GitHub PRs
from a checkbox-style list. Use this skill whenever the user says "standup",
"run the standup", "reconcile my worktrees", "consolidate worktrees", "merge
these branches together", "merge these PRs", "combine these worktrees and pull
requests", "what's everyone at", "have my worktrees check in", or wants several
branch-named agents to coordinate / resolve overlapping work into one
deliverable through a shared chat file — even if they don't say the word
"standup".
- turbopuffer: Build, query, and operate turbopuffer — the object-storage-native search engine for vector search (ANN/kNN), BM25 full-text search, hybrid search, and filtered retrieval. Use this skill whenever the user mentions turbopuffer or tpuf, a turbopuffer namespace or API key, or is building any retrieval layer that could run on it — semantic search, RAG retrieval, embeddings storage, vector databases, BM25/keyword search, hybrid search with rank fusion, multi-tenant search, or document filtering at scale. Also use it for turbopuffer operations work — writes/upserts, schema design, pagination/export, backups, branching, pinning, CMEK encryption, BYOC deployments, or debugging turbopuffer errors (HTTP 429 backpressure, 202 index-building, cold-query latency). Consult it even when the user doesn't name turbopuffer but their code imports @turbopuffer/turbopuffer or the turbopuffer SDK in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, C#, or Ruby.
- ux-designer: @thedotmack's personal landing page design system. Use this skill whenever building landing pages, marketing sites, product pages, or conversion-focused web experiences. Covers visual hierarchy, UX patterns, marketing copy, messaging strategy, and conversion optimization based on proven preferences and successful projects.
- what-the: What the? Use when the user wants a plain-English breakdown of something technical — the who, what, where, why, and when.
- wooow: Upload a PDF to wooow.now (WOWerpoint) and get back a shareable deck URL. Handles magic-link auth, admin-token auth, deck listing, deletion, and polling for conversion-ready. Use when the user says "wooow this", "upload to wooow", "make a wooow deck out of <file>", "share this PDF as slides", or any time they want a PDF turned into a wooow.now link.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- claude-mem:babysit: Watch a pull request or review cycle until it is ready to merge. Use when asked to babysit, monitor, or keep checking PR comments, reviews, and CI until all actionable issues are resolved.
- claude-mem:design-is: Audit a design against Dieter Rams' ten "Good design is..." principles, then hand off a /make-plan prompt for one of three outcomes — new design, refine design, or redesign. Use when the user says "audit this design", "design review", "check this UI against Rams", "is this UI good", "critique this design", "design audit", or asks for a critique that should lead to a plan.
- claude-mem:do: Execute a phased implementation plan using subagents. Use when asked to execute, run, or carry out a plan — especially one created by make-plan.
- claude-mem:how-it-works: Explain how claude-mem captures observations, when memory injection kicks in, and where data lives. Use when the user asks "how does claude-mem work?" or "what is this thing doing?".
- claude-mem:knowledge-agent: Build and query AI-powered knowledge bases from claude-mem observations. Use when users want to create focused "brains" from their observation history, ask questions about past work patterns, or compile expertise on specific topics.
- claude-mem:learn-codebase: Prime a codebase by reading every source file in full. Use when starting work on a new or unfamiliar project, or when the user asks to "learn the codebase", "read the codebase", "prime", or "get up to speed".
- claude-mem:make-plan: Create a detailed, phased implementation plan with documentation discovery. Use when asked to plan a feature, task, or multi-step implementation — especially before executing with do.
- claude-mem:mem-search: Search claude-mem's persistent cross-session memory database. Use when user asks "did we already solve this?", "how did we do X last time?", or needs work from previous sessions.
- claude-mem:oh-my-issues: Cluster a GitHub issue backlog by root cause into a small set of plan-master issues, redirect children with a standardized comment, and bundle architectural-fix PRs that close clusters atomically. Use when an issue tracker has accumulated dozens of reports that share underlying defects, when asked to triage / consolidate / cluster / dedupe issues, when asked to build a plan series or roadmap from open issues, or when routing a new incoming bug into an existing plan.
- claude-mem:pathfinder: Map a codebase into feature-grouped flowcharts, identify duplicated concerns across features, and propose a unified architecture. Use when asked to "find the ideal path," unify duplicated systems, or audit architecture before a refactor. Emits a proposed unified flowchart plus per-system /make-plan prompts.
- claude-mem:smart-explore: Token-optimized structural code search using tree-sitter AST parsing. Use instead of reading full files when you need to understand code structure, find functions, or explore a codebase efficiently.

- claude-mem:timeline-report: Generate a "Journey Into [Project]" narrative report analyzing a project's entire development history from claude-mem's timeline. Use when asked for a timeline report, project history analysis, development journey, or full project report.

Handles version increments across package.json, marketplace.json, plugin.json manifests, build verification, git tagging, GitHub releases, and changelog generation. NPM publishing (so `npx claude-mem@X.Y.Z` resolves) is handed off to the human maintainer, who raised npm security.
- claude-mem:weekly-digests: Generate a serial week-by-week narrative digest of a project's full claude-mem timeline. Splits the timeline into per-ISO-week files, then runs one consecutive subagent per week — each receiving the prior week's carry-forward block — to produce one chapter per ISO week of data. Use when asked for "weekly digests", "week-by-week story", "serial timeline", or "narrative chapters" of a project's history.

- ponytail:ponytail: Forces the laziest solution that actually works, simplest, shortest, most minimal. Channels a senior dev who has seen everything: question whether the task needs to exist at all (YAGNI), reach for the standard library before custom code, native platform features before dependencies, one line before fifty. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra. Use whenever the user says "ponytail", "be lazy", "lazy mode", "simplest solution", "minimal solution", "yagni", "do less", or "shortest path", and whenever they complain about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate, or unnecessary dependencies.
- ponytail:ponytail-audit: Whole-repo audit for over-engineering. Like ponytail-review, but scans the entire codebase instead of a diff: a ranked list of what to delete, simplify, or replace with stdlib/native equivalents. Use when the user says "audit this codebase", "audit for over-engineering", "what can I delete from this repo", "find bloat", "ponytail-audit", or "/ponytail-audit". One-shot report, does not apply fixes.
- ponytail:ponytail-debt: Harvest every `ponytail:` comment in the codebase into a debt ledger, so the deliberate shortcuts and deferrals ponytail leaves behind get tracked instead of rotting into "later means never". Use when the user says "ponytail debt", "/ponytail-debt", "what did ponytail defer", "list the shortcuts", "ponytail ledger", or "what did we mark to do later". One-shot report, changes nothing.
- ponytail:ponytail-gain: Show ponytail's measured impact as a compact scoreboard: less code, less cost, more speed, from the benchmark medians. One-shot display, not a persistent mode, and not a per-repo number. Trigger: /ponytail-gain, "ponytail gain", "what does ponytail save", "show ponytail impact", "ponytail scoreboard".
- ponytail:ponytail-help: Quick-reference card for all ponytail modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /ponytail-help, "ponytail help", "what ponytail commands", "how do I use ponytail".
- ponytail:ponytail-review: Code review focused exclusively on over-engineering. Finds what to delete: reinvented standard library, unneeded dependencies, speculative abstractions, dead flexibility. One line per finding: location, what to cut, what replaces it. Use when the user says "review for over-engineering", "what can we delete", "is this over-engineered", "simplify review", or invokes /ponytail-review. Complements correctness-focused review, this one only hunts complexity.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. #!/bin/sh
# No `set -e` around the claude call -- the `|| RC=$?` capture is the point.
# Prompt via stdin `-` per spawn setup-spa/main.ts:634; stderr split from transcript.
#
# DEV_PERSONA exists because prompt files read like a ticket handed to a human
# developer, and headless mode has no human to answer a clarifying question --
# without this, a model that defaults to asking before acting (observed on a
# weaker/free OpenRouter model) burns its one turn asking "what would you like
# me to do first?" and the run ends having done nothing. Appended (not
# replacing) the default system prompt so Claude Code's own tool-use
# instructions stay intact.
DEV_PERSONA="You are Dev, an autonomous senior software engineer working solo on this task. There is no human available to answer questions, approve a plan, or review your work before you finish. The prompt that follows is your only brief. Do not ask clarifying questions and do not pause waiting for a response -- make the most reasonable assumption for any ambiguity and keep going. Build the complete, working solution end-to-end in this session. Only stop once the task is fully implemented or you hit a hard blocker you cannot work around."
RC=0
mkdir -p /workspace/results
git init -q /workspace 2>/dev/null || true
claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions --append-system-prompt "$DEV_PERSONA" --output-format stream-json --verbose - \
  < /workspace/prompt.md \
  > /workspace/results/transcript.jsonl \
  2> /workspace/results/stderr.log || RC=$?
echo "$RC" > /workspace/results/exit-code
exit $RC

- Any other file that defines where "the project" the agent builds is supposed to live (is it /workspace itself, or a subdirectory like /workspace/project?)

<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>This confirms both. WORKDIR is `/workspace` — that's where `claude` runs and where the agent builds "the project" (comment confirms: "Working directory for agent projects"). Only `-v prompt.md:/workspace/prompt.md:ro` and `-v agentResultsDir:/workspace/results:rw` are mounted; nothing mounts `/workspace` itself. So generated project files sit in the container's writable layer and vanish on `docker rm`.

**Finding #1 — legitimate bug.** `container-manager.ts:82-84` mounts only two things:
```
'-v', `${promptFilePath}:/workspace/prompt.md:ro`,
'-v', `${agentResultsDir}:/workspace/results:rw`,
```
`WORKDIR /workspace` (Dockerfile:41, comment: "Working directory for agent projects") is where the agent's generated code lands, and it's entirely un-mounted — ephemeral. Nothing else in the repo mounts the rest of `/workspace` or copies project files into `results` post-run. The judge/smoke-runner has no way to see the built project.

**Finding #2 — legitimate bug.** `aggregator.ts:164-169`:
```js
function determineCompletionStatus(agentDir: string, files: string[]): string {
  if (files.includes('DONE.md')) return 'DONE';
  if (files.includes('CRASHED.md')) return 'CRASHED';
  if (files.includes('KILLED.md')) return 'KILLED';
  return 'INCOMPLETE';
}
```
`grep` across the repo shows `DONE.md`/`CRASHED.md`/`KILLED.md` are referenced *only* in `tests/aggregator.test.ts` (which manually writes them to fabricate fixtures) — never in `entrypoint.sh`, `container-manager.ts`, or any runtime code. `entrypoint.sh` only writes `exit-code`, which `aggregator.ts` never reads at all. Since `completion_status` feeds `generateSummary`'s `completionRate` (`aggregator.ts:390-393`, `r.completion_status === 'DONE'`), every real run — success or failure — is reported `INCOMPLETE` and completion rate is permanently 0.

Both Greptile findings are real, unfixed bugs, not already handled elsewhere. Fixes would need: (a) `container-manager.ts` to mount a project directory (e.g. `/workspace` itself, or add a dedicated `-v .../project:/workspace/project:rw` plus have the agent build there / entrypoint copy the tree into `results` post-run), and (b) `entrypoint.sh` to write `DONE.md`/`CRASHED.md` based on `$RC` (and something external, e.g. a timeout/kill supervisor, to write `KILLED.md`), or alternatively `aggregator.ts` should be changed to derive status from the `exit-code` file it already receives.</result>

file.content:
# Base: Node 20 + Bun (Anthropic's official devcontainer not publicly available)
# node:20-bookworm ships git, so no apt-get layer is needed.
# Headless Claude Code prep pattern adapted from OpenRouterLabs/spawn
# (sh/docker/claude.Dockerfile + agent-setup.ts:157-183, Apache-2.0).
FROM node:20-bookworm

ARG MEMORY_TYPE=vanilla
# Pinned for reproducibility -- a benchmark must NOT auto-update.
# Recorded in the run manifest as claude_code_version.
ARG CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION=2.1.199

# Install Bun
RUN curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash
ENV PATH="/root/.bun/bin:${PATH}"

# Install Claude Code CLI at the pinned version
RUN npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@${CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION}

# Pre-write headless config so no first-run wizard blocks the agent:
# settings.json grants bypassPermissions; .claude.json marks onboarding done
# and pre-trusts /workspace.
RUN mkdir -p /root/.claude \
 && printf '%s' '{"permissions":{"defaultMode":"bypassPermissions"}}' \
      > /root/.claude/settings.json \
 && printf '%s' '{"hasCompletedOnboarding":true,"bypassPermissionsModeAccepted":true,"projects":{"/workspace":{"hasTrustDialogAccepted":true}}}' \
      > /root/.claude.json \
 && chmod 600 /root/.claude.json

# Conditional: install claude-mem only when MEMORY_TYPE=claude-mem
RUN if [ "$MEMORY_TYPE" = "claude-mem" ]; then \
      npx claude-mem install; \
    fi

# Claude Code refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions under root unless the
# environment declares itself a sandbox; this image runs as root in an
# isolated container, which is exactly that case (verified: without this,
# claude exits 1 with "cannot be used with root/sudo privileges").
ENV IS_SANDBOX=1

# Working directory for agent projects
WORKDIR /workspace

# Copy entrypoint script
COPY entrypoint.sh /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh
RUN chmod +x /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh

# Prompt file mounted at runtime: /workspace/prompt.md
# Results directory mounted at runtime: /workspace/results/

ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]

#!/bin/sh
# No `set -e` around the claude call -- the `|| RC=$?` capture is the point.
# Prompt via stdin `-` per spawn setup-spa/main.ts:634; stderr split from transcript.
#
# DEV_PERSONA exists because prompt files read like a ticket handed to a human
# developer, and headless mode has no human to answer a clarifying question --
# without this, a model that defaults to asking before acting (observed on a
# weaker/free OpenRouter model) burns its one turn asking "what would you like
# me to do first?" and the run ends having done nothing. Appended (not
# replacing) the default system prompt so Claude Code's own tool-use
# instructions stay intact.
DEV_PERSONA="You are Dev, an autonomous senior software engineer working solo on this task. There is no human available to answer questions, approve a plan, or review your work before you finish. The prompt that follows is your only brief. Do not ask clarifying questions and do not pause waiting for a response -- make the most reasonable assumption for any ambiguity and keep going. Build the complete, working solution end-to-end in this session. Only stop once the task is fully implemented or you hit a hard blocker you cannot work around."
RC=0
mkdir -p /workspace/results
git init -q /workspace 2>/dev/null || true
claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions --append-system-prompt "$DEV_PERSONA" --output-format stream-json --verbose - \
  < /workspace/prompt.md \
  > /workspace/results/transcript.jsonl \
  2> /workspace/results/stderr.log || RC=$?
echo "$RC" > /workspace/results/exit-code
exit $RC

# Phase 4 — Live smoke test findings (2026-07-02)

One container, `benchmark-agent:vanilla`, real OpenRouter key, model `anthropic/claude-opus-4.6`,
trivial prompt ("Create a file named hello.txt containing exactly: arena-smoke-ok. Then stop."),
launched with the exact `launchAgent` env block (Phase 3 recipe). Container ran ~7s, exited 0.

## Verdict: **GO on exact-ledger costing**

Transcript assistant lines carry **OpenRouter `gen-…` ids directly in `message.id`**, and those ids
resolve on `GET /api/v1/generation` with the inference key, returning `total_cost`. Phase 6 should
sum `total_cost` over the unique `message.id` values per transcript (`cost_source: "openrouter_ledger"`),
reconciled against the `GET /api/v1/key` `usage_daily` delta. The token×live-pricing path is only a
fallback.

## The five questions

### 1. Transcript reality — `message.usage.cost` / `message.id` / `message.model`?

- `message.id`: **YES**, and it is the OpenRouter generation id itself (e.g.
  `gen-1783056340-M1Ht1ndvGfuVdps1pAKc`), not an Anthropic `msg_…` id. The documented gap
  ("X-Generation-Id header is invisible to transcripts") is moot: OpenRouter's `/messages`
  endpoint puts the gen-id in the response **body** id, which Claude Code writes to the transcript.
- `message.model`: **YES** — `anthropic/claude-4.6-opus-20260205` (see Q5).
- `message.usage.cost`: **NO.** Usage keys observed: `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`,
  `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation`, `server_tool_use`,
  `service_tier`, `inference_geo`, `speed`. No `cost`/`cost_details` extension survives into the
  transcript. Exact costing therefore goes through the gen-id → `/generation` lookup, not an
  inline field.

Sample assistant line (redacted; final turn, so its own usage block is zeroed — per-response
usage appears on the first assistant line of each API response):

```json
{"type": "assistant", "message": {"id": "gen-1783056343-Ch6YrTOXqLLBRGeg6ecy", "type": "message", "role": "assistant", "container": null, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Created `/workspace/hello.txt` with the requested content.", "citations": []}], "model": "anthropic/claude-4.6-opus-20260205", "stop_reason": null, "stop_details": null, "stop_sequence": null, "usage": {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0, "cache_creation_input_tokens": null, "cache_read_input_tokens": null, "cache_creation": null, "inference_geo": null, "server_tool_use": null, "service_tier": null, "speed": "standard"}, "provider": "Anthropic", "context_management": null}, "parent_tool_use_id": null, "session_id": "[REDACTED-UUID]", "uuid": "[REDACTED-UUID]"}
```

Note the bonus `"provider": "Anthropic"` field on the message object.

### 2. Ledger id — does the transcript id resolve on `GET /api/v1/generation`?

**YES — both gen-ids, HTTP 200 with the inference key:**

| field | gen-1783056340-M1Ht… | gen-1783056343-Ch6Y… |
|---|---|---|
| `total_cost` | 0.213075 | 0.2116175 |
| `provider_name` | Anthropic | Anthropic |
| `model` | anthropic/claude-4.6-opus-20260205 | anthropic/claude-4.6-opus-20260205 |
| `app_id` | 4280272 | 4280272 |
| `origin` | https://github.com/thedotmack/ArenaBench | (same) |
| `native_tokens_prompt` / `_completion` | 33706 / 97 | 33795 / 16 |
| `cache_discount` | -0.04212 | -0.0422425 |
| `is_byok` | false | false |
| `upstream_id` | msg_01Bd… | msg_016V… |

The Anthropic `msg_…` id appears only as `upstream_id` **inside** the generation record — it never
appears in the transcript, and no separate `/generation?id=msg_…` probe was needed since gen-ids
are directly available.

Caveat: the background haiku call (`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL`, 537 in / 16 out tokens per the
result line's `modelUsage`) leaves **no gen-id in the transcript**, so ledger-summed cost misses it

---
id: "09-url-shortener"
title: "URL Shortener API"
category: api
timeout_hint: "4h"
industry_baseline:
  source: none
  reference_cost_usd: null
  reference_duration_seconds: null
  reference_architecture: null
smoke_tests:
  - name: "health_check"
    command: "curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:3000"
    expected: "status:200"
  - name: "shorten_url"
    command: "curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/shorten -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{\"url\":\"https://example.com\"}'"
    expected: "contains:alias"
  - name: "get_stats"
    command: "curl -s http://localhost:3000/stats/test"
    expected: "contains:count"
---

# URL Shortener API

Build a URL shortener REST API service. Users can submit long URLs and receive short aliases. Visiting the short alias redirects to the original URL. Stats endpoint tracks visit counts.

## Requirements

### Core Features
1. **Shorten URL**: Accept a long URL and return a short alias (auto-generated or custom)
2. **Redirect**: Visiting `GET /:alias` redirects (HTTP 302) to the original URL
3. **Statistics**: Track visit counts per alias, including total visits and visits over time
4. **Custom Aliases**: Optionally allow users to specify a custom alias (validate uniqueness)
5. **Expiration**: Optional TTL for short URLs (default: never expires)

### Technical Requirements
- Serves on **port 3000**
- Node.js backend with Express or similar
- SQLite or in-memory storage
- Short aliases: 6-8 alphanumeric characters, URL-safe
- Rate limiting on the shorten endpoint (e.g., 100 requests per minute per IP)

### API Endpoints
- `GET /` — Health check / API info page
- `POST /shorten` — Create short URL
  - Body: `{ "url": "https://...", "custom_alias": "optional", "ttl_seconds": 0 }`
  - Response: `{ "alias": "abc123", "short_url": "http://localhost:3000/abc123", "original_url": "https://..." }`
- `GET /:alias` — Redirect to original URL (HTTP 302)
- `GET /stats/:alias` — Get visit statistics
  - Response: `{ "alias": "abc123", "original_url": "https://...", "count": 42, "created_at": "...", "last_visited": "..." }`

### Data Model
- **ShortURL**: id, alias (unique), original_url, created_at, expires_at, visit_count
- **Visit**: id, short_url_id, visited_at, ip_address, user_agent

### Error Handling
- Invalid URL format: 400 with descriptive message
- Alias already taken: 409 Conflict
- Alias not found: 404
- Expired alias: 410 Gone

## Testable Deliverables
- Server starts on port 3000
- POST /shorten with a valid URL returns an alias
- GET /:alias redirects to the original URL
- GET /stats/:alias returns visit count
- Custom alias works when provided and available
- Duplicate custom alias returns 409

Yes, confirmed working — three ways:

1. **Live evidence in this very session**: every time I `Read` a file this session that already had prior observations, a `PreToolUse:Read hook additional context` block appeared with relevant history — e.g. `entrypoint.sh` surfaced the earlier "fatal startup bug" note, `container-manager.ts` surfaced the OpenRouter env-block notes, and just now `09-url-shortener.md` surfaced the A/B test architecture note.

> - **Need details on a past observation?** get_observations([IDs]) — ~300 tokens each.
> - **Need a structural map first?** smart_outline("...") — line numbers only, cheaper than re-reading.

So it's an additive nudge with escape hatches to cheaper tools, not a replacement of the file read.

content.text:
This is really a Claude Code CLI internals question, not a Claude API/SDK integration question — the `claude-api` skill's docs don't cover it. Answering from what's directly confirmed in this session plus general knowledge of Claude Code, flagging confidence levels:

**What it controls:** `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` (and its siblings `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL`) override which underlying model string Claude Code substitutes whenever it internally reaches for the "haiku tier" — it's a model-string remap, not a claude-mem-specific hook.

**Is it claude-mem-only, or does Claude Code itself use haiku internally?** Confirmed empirically in this session: it's Claude Code itself, not claude-mem. In the test I just ran, both the `cmem-` (claude-mem installed) and `vanilla-` (no claude-mem) containers showed an identical `anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5` line in their transcript's `modelUsage` — same exact `inputTokens: 1351`, `outputTokens: 14`, `costUSD: 0.0071` in both. Since claude-mem isn't even installed in the vanilla image, that call has to be coming from Claude Code's own baseline behavior (almost certainly something like session/conversation-summary generation), not from a plugin. `container-manager.ts` in this repo sets the env var unconditionally for both arms for exactly this reason.

**If unset while `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at a custom gateway and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is empty:** I don't have authoritative documentation confirming the exact failure mode, so treat this as reasoned inference, not a cited fact. `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`/`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` govern *where the request goes and how it authenticates* — they don't change *which model string Claude Code fills in* for its internal haiku-tier call. Without the override, Claude Code likely falls back to a hardcoded Anthropic-native model ID (e.g. `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`) for that internal call. Sent as the `model` field to a gateway like OpenRouter, which expects vendor-prefixed slugs (`anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5`), that ID would very plausibly be rejected — so the specific internal call fails/errors rather than silently degrading, while the main coding-model calls (which do get an explicit `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` override) keep working fine. This lines up with this project's own history: an earlier session's notes flagged `container-manager.ts` as initially missing `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`/`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` injection as a "critical bug," and the fix that followed hardcoded `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL` for every arm — consistent with this exact failure mode having been hit and worked around.

If you want a definitive answer rather than inference, that's a good question for the `claude-code-guide` agent, which has access to Claude Code's actual settings/CLI documentation.

Confirmed — I reported the wrong number. Corrected:

| | Transcript's self-reported `total_cost_usd` (what I quoted before) | **Actual OpenRouter billed cost** (ledger, `GET /api/v1/generation` summed per gen-id) |
|---|---|---|
| `cmem-09-url-shortener-1` | $0.724 | **$0.478** |
| `vanilla-09-url-shortener-1` | $0.682 | **$0.450** |
| **Total** | **$1.406** | **$0.928** |

I overstated the real cost by ~52% by quoting Claude Code's self-reported `total_cost_usd`, which — per this repo's own Phase 4 finding — is priced at Anthropic-direct rates, not actual OpenRouter rates. The ledger figures above are the real, billed-by-OpenRouter numbers, pulled per unique generation ID (20 for cmem, 22 for vanilla — all `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-20260630`).

One caveat carried over from that same finding: the background Haiku call doesn't get a `gen-` ID in the transcript, so it's not in this ledger total — it's a separate ~$0.007 (self-reported, likely also somewhat inflated) that's too small to move these numbers meaningfully.

**Real total spend for this test: ~$0.93**, not the ~$1.41 I said earlier.
